Hand in hand, Christine and Raoul rushed downstairs from the roof, stopping on the eighth floor of the opera house. As they started running through a corridor, a mysterious figure blocked their way. He pointed in another direction. "Go that way! Hurry!"
"Who was that?" Raoul glanced behind them as Christine dragged him away.
"The Persian! He's always wandering around the opera house, but no one knows much about him. Come on!"
Christine found another staircase and led Raoul to her dressing room. She locked the door.
"Erik has a powerful hold over you," Raoul said. "Are you sure you'll be ready to elope with me tomorrow night?"
Christine nodded. "After listening to my performance, Erik will be waiting for me in his house by the lake. It'll be the perfect time to escape."
"And how were you supposed to get to Erik's house—through your mirror?"

"No," Christine said. "I don't know how to use the mirror as a passageway." She opened a box and removed an enormous key. "But with this key, I can go outside and open some gates. They lead to an underground passage and the lake."
Christine held up the key, her eyes widening in horror as she stared at her left hand. "Oh no!"
"What's wrong, darling?"

"I've lost Erik's ring! He said, 'I give you this ring and your freedom on the condition that the ring remains on your finger. As long as you wear it, you'll be protected against all danger, and I'll remain your friend. But woe to you if you ever lose it!' Oh, Raoul, where is it?"
The couple searched every inch of Christine's dressing room but couldn't find the ring.
Christine was growing more frantic by the minute. "It must have slipped off my finger on the roof or while we were running downstairs. Oh, terrible things are going to happen!"
"Let's leave at once," Raoul insisted, taking Christine's hands in his.

"No," Christine protested, pulling her hands away. "I must sing for Erik one last time tomorrow night. It's the least I can do for him because it'll break his heart when I run away with you. Go home, Raoul! I'll be waiting here tomorrow night at midnight."
Reluctantly Raoul went home, greatly upset by all that Christine had said. He was still thinking about the situation when he went downstairs for breakfast the next morning.
His brother, Philippe, slapped a newspaper down on the table and pointed to a short item.

The latest rumor is that Mademoiselle Christine Daaé, the opera singer, is engaged to Raoul, Viscount de Chagny. We hear that a certain count is not rejoicing over his younger brother's happy announcement and has vowed to prevent the marriage. Will this tale end with the viscount leading his love to the altar, or will it, like so many operas, have a sad and tragic ending?
"What's going on, Raoul?" Philippe demanded. "All of Paris is talking about you and . . . and that woman! You're making our family look ridiculous!"
It was impossible for Raoul to explain this situation to Philippe, but he tried his best. "If I don't save Christine from Erik, she'll be lost forever. So I will save her."
"Who is this Erik?"
"My rival, who lives in an opera house cellar near the lake and—"
"What are you babbling about?" Philippe snapped.
"Never mind. I'm going to elope with Christine tonight. Good-bye, Philippe."
"If you try anything so foolish, I'll know how to stop you!" Philippe said as Raoul strode from the room.
For the rest of the day, Raoul devoted himself to his preparations. The horses, the carriage, the coachman, the luggage, the food and money for the journey—everything had to be arranged.

At nine o'clock Raoul's carriage took its place in a line of horse-drawn vehicles outside the opera house, including his brother's. The curtains in Raoul's carriage were drawn so he didn't see a shadow in a long black coat and soft felt hat pass along the sidewalk. The figure examined Raoul's carriage and horses before slipping off into the darkness. Some people later said they thought the shadow was Raoul, although he usually wore a top hat to the opera. Others speculated that the shadow was the phantom of the opera.
Raoul entered the theater and took a seat near the stage without looking up at Philippe's box. The opera that night was Faust , and Christine was scheduled to sing the role of Marguerite.
Meanwhile the audience was abuzz with talk of the engagement announcement in the newspaper.
"Christine Daaé is aiming rather high for a peasant girl who happens to have a nice voice," one woman said to another.
Her friend looked up at Philippe's box, where the count sat alone. "I wonder where the viscount is tonight."
As the opera started, Philippe kept his eyes on the stage, ignoring the people staring at him and gossiping.
From the moment Christine stepped onstage, she sensed some antagonism from the audience, and her confidence wavered.
"I hope she doesn't start to croak," one man whispered to his wife.

Just then Carlotta herself made a sensational entrance as she took a seat at the front of one of the boxes. Poor Christine raised her eyes and recognized her rival at once. However, instead of intimidating the young singer, Carlotta inspired Christine to triumph once again. From that moment Christine sang with all her heart and soul.
Christine sang with her arms outstretched, the glory of the music inspiring her. Seeing her looking so beautiful and singing so wonderfully, Raoul stood up, facing his beloved.
Christine went on. At that moment the stage was plunged into darkness. It all happened so quickly that the audience barely had time to react.
At once the gas was relit, and the stage was illuminated again. But Christine was nowhere to be seen. It was as if an angel had really carried her off!

Raoul uttered a cry of agony, while Philippe sprang to his feet. People looked from the stage to Philippe to Raoul and wondered if this curious incident were connected to the newspaper story. The curtain dropped, and both men left their seats while the rest of the audience waited for some news.

At last the curtain rose again, and the conductor stepped onstage. "Ladies and gentleman, something terrible has happened—our leading lady has disappeared before our eyes, and nobody knows where she is!"

The managers of the opera house had been agitated for some time. Awhile back they'd found a note from the ghost in their office, saying their first payment of twenty thousand francs was due. The ghost instructed them to put the money into the envelope he'd enclosed. They were told to seal it with wax before handing it to the usher Madame Giry to place in box five.

Moncharmin and Richard did as they were told. Then they spent the evening watching the ghost's box to see who would pick up the envelope. When no one did, they went to the box and opened the envelope. Inside they found twenty thousand francs—but in play money! The seal on the envelope wasn't broken. So how had the money been replaced?
Now, on the night when Christine was singing the role of Marguerite, it was time for another payment. The opera ghost had written, saying they should follow the same procedure.
"I've sent for Madame Giry because she must know what's really going on with these payments," Richard said to Moncharmin.
The usher soon arrived at their office. "I assume you have another envelope for the ghost that you'd like me to deliver," she said.
"Yes, and we want to talk to you about it." Richard picked up the envelope full of francs.
"Anything at all, gentlemen," Madame Giry said.
"We're not fools." Richard's expression hardened, and his voice grew harsh. "We know the opera ghost doesn't exist. You must be the accomplice of some con man. Tell us his name at once!"
"I don't understand . . . an accomplice . . . what?" Madame Giry looked genuinely confused.
"How much does this so-called ghost give you when you leave the envelope in his box?" Richard said.
"Ten francs."
"That's not much," Moncharmin said.

"That's not all." Madame Giry hesitated before she spoke. "The ghost doesn't like me to talk about him, but awhile back he left me a letter in box five. In red ink he'd written a list of famous dancers and the years they'd married royalty. Next to a future year—1885—was my daughter Meg's name, followed by one word: empress!"

Exhausted by her confession, Madame Giry flopped into a chair. "Before that letter I'd only half-believed in the opera ghost. After he declared that my Meg would one day marry the emperor, I totally believed in him."
"You've never seen the ghost, yet you believe everything he says, no matter how improbable?" Moncharmin asked.

"Yes! I told the ghost, if Meg's going to become empress, she'll need to attract the attention of the emperor. The phantom said something to the previous managers, and Meg immediately started getting better roles."
Richard gave Moncharmin a skeptical look. "And now, madame, I'll tell you another reason I sent for you. I'm going to have you arrested for the theft of twenty thousand francs!"
Madame Giry popped up from her chair and slapped Richard across the face. Shocked, he dropped the envelope, which opened, scattering the notes.
"Look at all that money!" Madame Giry exclaimed. The managers dropped to the floor, quickly gathering up the notes. "I had no idea what was in that envelope!"
Richard clutched the envelope tightly as he stood up. "What happened to the money we gave you last time?"
"If anyone should know, it's you, Monsieur Richard!" Madame Giry said. "Because I put the envelope in the pocket of your coattail!"
"What?" Richard made a move toward Madame Giry.
"Here, let me take over," Moncharmin said, stepping between his partner and the usher. "Now please explain what you did with the envelope containing the real money."
"I told you—I put it in Monsieur Richard's pocket. The one I left in box five was an identical envelope, which the ghost gave me beforehand and I slipped up my sleeve."

At this point, Madame Giry took from her sleeve an envelope that matched the one Richard was holding. The managers turned the envelope over and saw it was sealed with wax stamped with their own seal. Upon opening it, they found twenty thousand francs in play money.
"Amazing!" Moncharmin said. "How did he get our seal?"
"Everyone's a magician these days!" Richard grumbled.
"Why do you think the ghost went to all this trouble?" Moncharmin said.

"He doesn't want anyone to see him picking up the envelope," Madame Giry said. "So after you gave me the one with the real money, I kept it up my sleeve. When I went to the ballet foyer to visit Meg, it was crowded as always, and easy for me to slip behind Monsieur Richard. That's when I put the envelope into the tail pocket of his coat."
Richard rolled his eyes with disbelief. "You're lying! I spent that whole evening watching box five and the envelope you put there. I didn't go near the ballet foyer!"
Madame Giry gave a satisfied smile. "I didn't give you the envelope that night. I waited until the next night when you were busy greeting the mayor."
"Wait a minute!" Richard said. "I do remember you bumping against me. Was that when it happened?"
Madame Giry nodded. "You didn't even know the real money was in your pocket. All the ghost had to do was come up behind you and take it."
"Well, that's not going to happen tonight!" Richard called for the managers' assistant. "Mercier, come here! Lock Madame Giry in your office so she can't communicate with her ghost friend."
Mercier escorted the protesting usher away while the managers discussed what to do.
"We need to get to the bottom of this mystery," Moncharmin said. "For now, the safest thing to do is lock ourselves in the office until after the performance."
Richard nodded.

"When Mercier returns," Moncharmin went on, "let's ask him for a safety pin to fasten the envelope—and the money—to your pocket. If the ghost tries to remove the envelope, you'll feel his hand in your pocket!"

The managers were in their office all evening, so they were unaware of Christine's dramatic disappearance. Before they left for the night, Richard felt his pocket to be sure the money was still there.
"I can feel the safety pin, but the envelope's gone!" Richard tore off his coat and turned his pocket inside out. It was empty!
Moncharmin gasped. "The ghost must have been here!"
"We would have seen him!" Richard said.
At that moment Mercier knocked on the office door, shouting something about Christine. But the managers were too distraught about their twenty thousand francs to comprehend what he was saying.
When Christine disappeared, Raoul rushed onto the stage, desperately hoping to find her unharmed.
"Christine! Christine!" Raoul shouted. "Oh, why don't you answer? Are you alive?"
Raoul wondered if Christine was calling him from the opera house cellars. He tried to go below the stage, but no one was allowed there, so he headed backstage instead.

"Erik must have discovered we were planning to elope," Raoul thought, hurrying to Christine's dressing room. "He's furious that Christine has broken her promise to return to him, and this is his terrible revenge."

Tears filled Raoul's eyes as he entered Christine's dressing room and saw the clothes she'd laid out for their flight. Raoul attacked the mirror, frantically searching for a lever or button to open the glass into the dark world beyond. Alas, the mirror apparently obeyed no one except Erik.

"The key!" Raoul suddenly remembered Christine mentioning gates that opened into an underground passage. The box that held the key was empty, so Raoul rushed outside to the street where the gates were located. Peering through locked gates, he saw only darkness beyond.
He groaned with frustration. "Perhaps someone has found Christine by now," he thought, dashing back into the opera house and onto the stage.
He approached two men who were deep in conversation. "Excuse me, gentlemen, can you tell me where Christine is?"
"This is the person you should ask," said Mercier, the managers' assistant, introducing Raoul to Monsieur Mifroid, the police commissioner.
"Delighted to meet you, Viscount," Mifroid said. "Now where are the managers?"
"In their office," Mercier said. "I tried to tell them about Christine, but they seemed too distracted by something else to understand what I was saying."
"Then let's go to their office," Mifroid said.
"I'll join you in a few minutes," said Mercier. He wanted to release Madame Giry from his own office before Mifroid started investigating that situation too.
Raoul accompanied the police commissioner to the managers' office. He was about to follow Mifroid inside when someone laid a hand on his shoulder.
"Erik's secrets are nobody's business but his own!" the Persian whispered.
Before Raoul could respond, the Persian bowed and disappeared. Still pondering the mysterious man's comment, Raoul hurried into the office.
"Is Christine here?" Mifroid asked the managers.
"No, why would she be here when she should be onstage?" Richard asked.
"Because she disappeared in the middle of the performance," Mifroid said.
"What?" Moncharmin said. "In the middle of the performance?"
"Yes, I was told she vanished at the moment she was addressing an angel," the police commissioner said. "But I doubt she was carried off by an angel."
"And I'm sure she was carried off by an angel who lives in the opera house!" Raoul announced.
Everyone turned to look at him.
"An angel who lives in the opera house?" Mifroid struggled to hide a smile while the two managers looked at each other in astonishment.
"His name is Erik, and he's the Angel of Music!" Raoul said.
"The Angel of Music? Are you serious?" The police commissioner laughed and turned back to the managers. "Do you gentlemen have an Angel of Music on the premises?"
Richard and Moncharmin shook their heads without speaking.
"I'm sure you've heard of the opera ghost," Raoul said to the managers. "Well, I can confidently state that the opera ghost and the Angel of Music are the same person."
Mifroid looked Raoul right in the eye. "I beg your pardon, monsieur, but are you making fun of us? And if not, what's all this about an opera ghost?"
"Ask them!" Raoul pointed to the managers.
"Do you know the opera ghost?" Mifroid asked the managers.
The managers were reluctant to say anything, but finally Richard spoke. "No, we don't know him, but we wish we did because he robbed us of twenty thousand francs tonight!"

Mifroid ran his fingers through his hair. "A ghost who steals twenty thousand francs and kidnaps a singer the same night is one busy fellow! Let's deal with the singer first. Viscount de Chagny, have you ever seen this Erik?"
"Yes, in a graveyard."
Mifroid lifted his eyebrows. "Of course. That's where ghosts usually hang out. And what were you doing in this graveyard?"
"I know my story will seem strange, but you must listen because the life of the woman I love is at stake."
As Raoul described the ghost playing the violin in Perros-Guirec, his listeners began to question his sanity. Before Raoul could finish his story, a man entered the office and whispered to Mifroid.
"I see," Mifroid said to the man, who appeared to be a detective. "Good work."

As the man left, Mifroid turned his attention to Raoul. "I understand that you intended to elope with Christine tonight and that a carriage was ready outside the opera house. Did you know there were three other carriages in front of yours?"
"I didn't really pay attention," Raoul said.
"Your carriage is still there, as are the carriages of two opera performers, Sorelli and Carlotta, but your brother's carriage is gone."
"What does that have to do with me?"
"Your brother was opposed to your marriage to Christine, wasn't he?"
Raoul was bewildered by the police commissioner's line of questioning. "Yes, but I don't see how that concerns anyone outside my family."
"Well, I've just received information that the count has outsmarted you. Your brother is the one who has carried off Christine!"
"That's impossible!" Raoul pressed his hand to his heart. "Are you sure?"
"We don't know how he snatched Christine from the stage, but immediately afterward his carriage was seen traveling across Paris at a furious pace."
"Across Paris?" Raoul said. "What do you mean?"
"It was leaving the city."
"Oh no! I must catch them!" cried Raoul, and he dashed from the office.

"And bring back Christine to us!" Mifroid called after Raoul. Then he addressed the managers with a satisfied smile. "I have no idea whether the count has carried off Christine or not, but right now no one is more anxious to find her than Raoul. Let me tell you something about police work: it's really quite simple if you get other people to do your job for you!"
But Mifroid wouldn't have been so smug if he'd known that Raoul never made it outside. As soon as Raoul left the office, a tall figure blocked his path.
"Where are you going in such a hurry, Monsieur de Chagny?" the Persian asked.
"Please answer me, sir!" the Persian said, keeping pace with Raoul, who was hurrying away from the managers' office. "Where are you going in such a rush?"

"To Christine's assistance, sir," Raoul replied without slowing down. "Mifroid, the police commissioner, said my brother has abducted her, and no one knows where he's taking her. I must get my carriage and pursue them."
"If you want to rescue Christine, you'll find her in the opera house," the Persian said.
Raoul stopped and turned to him in surprise. "You mean she's here with Erik?"
The Persian nodded.
Raoul was skeptical of this man he'd only just met. His eyes narrowed as he demanded, "How do you know this?"
"I was at the performance tonight, and only Erik could have conceived of an abduction like that, snatching Christine right from the stage." The Persian sighed. "I recognized the monster's touch."
"So you're acquainted with Erik?" Raoul said.
The Persian sighed again. "Yes, I first encountered him in my role as chief of police in my country."
"Sir," Raoul said, "I don't know what your intentions are, but can you do anything to help me, to help Christine?"
"I can attempt to take you to her . . . and to him."
"If you can do that, I'll be eternally grateful, but I must ask one question," Raoul said, pausing for a moment. "Do you think it's possible that my brother abducted Christine?"
"No," the Persian said, shaking his head. "From what I've heard about your brother, he isn't capable of a kidnapping, never mind a dramatic one."

Raoul nodded in agreement. He had noticed that the Persian, unlike Mifroid, hadn't laughed at the mention of Erik. "I believe you know Erik is real and a threat to Christine," Raoul said. "So I place myself in your hands—take me to Christine and Erik."
"Silence!" The Persian appeared to be listening to distant sounds in the opera house. "We must avoid using his name in case he overhears us."
Raoul looked around in alarm. "Do you think he's nearby?"
"I don't know, but it's quite possible he's here in this wall or floor or ceiling."

The Persian led Raoul through passages that Raoul had never seen before. After traveling up and down several staircases, they stopped at a door, which the Persian opened with a master key. Across from the door was the entrance to Christine's dressing room.
Raoul was impressed—he hadn't realized this route to her dressing room even existed. "You know the opera house so well, sir."
"Not half as well as he does," the Persian muttered as they entered Christine's room and shut the door.
The Persian pressed his ear against one wall and coughed softly. There was the sound of a person stirring, and seconds later, someone tapped on the door.
"I've summoned my servant, Darius, who was waiting in the storage room next door," the Persian explained.
A man wearing a long overcoat entered the room. He bowed, took a richly carved case from under his coat, placed it on Christine's dressing table, bowed again, and went to the door.
"Darius, did anyone see you come in here?" the Persian asked.
"No."
"Then don't let anyone see you leave."
Darius opened the door, glanced up and down the passage, and quickly disappeared.

The Persian opened the case, which contained two pistols. "When Christine was abducted, I sent word to Darius to bring these." He handed a pistol to Raoul. "We'll be fighting the most terrifying enemy you can imagine, but you must do it for Christine's sake. You love her, don't you?"
"I worship the ground she walks on!" Raoul declared. "But you don't even know Christine, so why are you ready to risk your life for her? You must hate Erik."
"No, I don't hate him," the Persian said, shaking his head sadly. "I've forgiven him for the harm he's done to me, but that's a story for another time."
"You say he's a monster," Raoul said, "yet I detect in you the same pity for him that Christine has. Her pity nearly drove me to despair."

The Persian did not reply. Instead he fetched a stool and set it in front of the wall opposite the large mirror. He climbed onto the stool and seemed to be looking for something in the pattern of the wallpaper. At last he tapped a spot. "There it is—in half a minute, we'll be on our way to his house."
The Persian turned around and jumped off the stool. He crossed the room and pressed his hand against the mirror. "It's not moving yet."
"Are we going through the mirror?" Raoul asked. "I saw Christine do that on the night of the masked ball."
"And what did you think of that?"
"I thought I was seeing things!" Raoul said.

"Or that it was some new trick of the opera ghost's." The Persian laughed as he pressed his hand on the mirror again. "Oh, if only we were dealing with a ghost, things would be much simpler. We must make ourselves as invisible as possible. Cover the front of your white shirt as much as you can with your coat."
Raoul followed the Persian’s instructions. "Why isn't the mirror opening?"
"It doesn't open; it turns," the Persian said. "When you press the button in this room, the mechanism takes time to work. But when he's behind the wall, he can make the mirror turn instantly."
"That's probably what happened on the night of the masked ball."
"If you watch, you'll see the mirror rise a few inches and then shift a little from left to right. It will then be on a pivot and swing around."
"The mirror still isn't doing anything!" Raoul was impatient to get going.
"It will—unless, of course, he's disabled the mechanism because he knows we're coming."
"And if he's done that, what about Christine?"

"We'll do all that's humanly possible to save her, although he may stop us before we reach her. He commands the walls, the doors, and the trapdoors. In my country, he was known as the man who loves trapdoors."
"But why do the walls and doors obey him?" Raoul asked, puzzled. "He didn't build them."
"Actually, he did build them! And his house lies within the walls of the opera house cellars."

Before Raoul could ask another question, the mirror rose and shifted sideways. As the Persian pulled Raoul close to him, the mirror turned like a shimmering revolving door. The two men were hurled from the dressing room into total darkness.

Raoul and the Persian stood motionless, each holding his breath as the mirrored wall slid back into place. Then the Persian fumbled in the dark until he found a lantern he'd hidden. Turning it on, he shined a dim light down the passage.
"This must be the way that Erik reached Christine's dressing room," Raoul said.

The Persian dropped to his knees and concentrated his light on the floor. He found what he was looking for, and Raoul heard a faint click. A square opening appeared in the floor, as if a window had opened on the opera house cellars.
Turning off his lantern, the Persian whispered, "Follow me." The Persian hung by his hands from the opening and dropped into the cellar below.
Raoul hesitated for a second, wondering if this were some kind of trap. "But the Persian wouldn't have given me a pistol if he intended to harm me," he decided.
"Hurry up!" the Persian said.
Slipping through the opening, Raoul landed on the floor. As the Persian led him through the labyrinth of passages, Raoul wondered what he'd have done without his guide.
Somewhere in the third cellar, they heard a man shouting. "All door shutters onstage! The police commissioner wants all door shutters onstage!"
The Persian pulled Raoul behind a piece of scenery. Raoul heard footsteps and saw shadows gliding through the dimly lit cellar.
"Who are the door shutters?" Raoul asked.

"Retired stagehands," the Persian said. "They're paid to shut doors to protect the singers' voices from drafts. It's good they'll be onstage for a while. We wouldn't want to trip over one of them taking a nap."
The two men were not alone for long because they soon spotted more shadows, carrying lanterns.
"I don't know who they are," the Persian said. "There are too many people here. Let's go down these stairs."
The Persian seemed to relax once they reached the fifth cellar, but that lasted only a few minutes. Something moved in the darkness ahead of them.
"Lie flat on your stomach!" the Persian whispered.
The two men hit the floor just as a person without a lantern approached them. There was still enough light that Raoul could see someone wrapped in a cloak.
"Was that him? " Raoul asked when the man was out of sight.
"If it had been him, we'd have seen his eyes glowing in the dark. That's more or less our safeguard tonight—unless he sneaks up behind us. Then we're dead men."
Raoul gulped. "What do you mean?" Before the Persian could answer, a startling sight appeared in the distance—a head of fire!

The Persian looked surprised too. "Oh, I guess that fireman really did see a flaming head awhile back," he said. "I thought I knew most of his tricks but not this one. Come on! We'll be safer if we run."
The two men fled down the long passage ahead of them.
"He rarely comes to this part of the opera house," the Persian said. "This side doesn't lead to his house or the lake. Perhaps he knows we're after him even though I promised to leave him alone."
"Why did you promise—"
"Hush! I'll tell you later."
The Persian pulled Raoul to a stop, and both men turned to look behind them.
"Oh, no!" Raoul said. "The head is still there—and getting closer! It must be running after us! And listen, what's that noise?"

Neither Raoul nor the Persian could identify the scratching, skittering sound that accompanied the flaming head. As the head drew closer, they could see round, staring eyes above a large nose and mouth. The two men ran, but the head was soon right behind them. Now Raoul knew what the sound was. He shouted and stamped his feet as small creatures with little legs scurried around his shoes. The Persian raised his pistol, ready to fire.
"Don't move!" the head of fire cried out. "Whatever you do, don't come after me! I'm the ratcatcher. Let me pass with my rats."
The flaming head and the rats disappeared, vanishing into the darkness. Raoul let out a sigh of relief, and the Persian laughed.
"I should have remembered the opera house has a ratcatcher," the Persian said. "His lantern was focused on his face, so he wouldn't scare the rats. That's why he looked so strange."

The Persian wanted to rest for a moment, but Raoul was full of questions and plans. "Are we very far from the lake now? When will we get there? When we arrive, we'll call out, and Christine will hear us. Of course, he'll hear us too, but he knows you, so we'll—"

"Hush!" the Persian interrupted. "We'll never enter his house from the lake because it's too well-guarded by a siren, a creature who sings the most beautiful music. I would have been killed there myself if he hadn't recognized me. Never go near the lake, and above all, cover your ears if you hear the siren singing. I've never been inside his house—"
"What?" Raoul exploded with anger and impatience. "Then how can you help Christine?"
The Persian tried to calm the young man. "Our only hope is to enter the house unnoticed by him."
"But how do we enter the house without crossing the lake?"

"I know the exact spot—even though I've never used it myself. It's where the old scenery is stored, the place where Joseph Buquet's body was found. We must return to the third cellar and hope that everyone has left by now so we can use the secret entrance."
Raoul followed his guide back up to the third cellar, where they squeezed between two old sets—a farmhouse and a throne room.
"Sit down and rest for a few minutes," the Persian said, taking a seat on the floor and inviting Raoul to sit next to him.
"Why?" Raoul remained standing. "Every minute we waste is another minute Christine is a prisoner."
"Before we enter his house—a most dangerous place—I want to tell you my history with him. That way you'll trust me and do everything I say."
"Aren't you worried he'll overhear us?"
The Persian shook his head. "This floor is made of stone, as are the walls of his house, which means once we enter, no one outside the house will hear our screams."
Raoul sighed impatiently as he sat next to the Persian on the floor of the third cellar. "I'll listen to your story but only so you'll lead me to Christine."

The Persian nodded and began his tale. "I'd frequently asked Erik to show me his house on the lake, but he refused. Although I spied on him from the opposite shore, it was always too dark to see the entrance and how he opened it. One day, thinking I was alone, I stepped into the boat and began to row. The house itself was invisible from the lake because it was hidden behind the cellar wall. Immediately the silence was broken by soft singing that rose from the waters and surrounded me."
Raoul's eyes widened in fear. "The siren!"

The Persian nodded. "The voice followed me as I rowed, but it was so lovely that I wasn't alarmed. On the contrary, I wanted to discover the source of that sweet and enticing music. I leaned out of the boat and over the water—"
"Oh, no!" Raoul's hurry to find Christine was temporarily forgotten as he got caught up in the Persian's story.

"Although I was in the middle of the lake," the Persian continued, "I felt perfectly safe because the water was calm. I had no doubt that I was face-to-face with some new trick of Erik's. But this trick was so perfect that I didn't care how he'd created it. I only wanted to get closer to the music, so I leaned and leaned—"
"And the boat tipped over?" Raoul asked.

The Persian shook his head. "Suddenly two huge arms reached up and seized me by the neck. I was dragged underwater and would have drowned if I hadn't fought back. Gasping for air, I reached the surface and cried out. Fortunately, Erik recognized my voice, and instead of drowning me, he rescued me and laid me on the edge of the lake."
"Was he upset that you were trying to find his house?"

"Yes, he was very angry. He said, 'I never invited you! I don't want you here!' I tried to pacify him by asking how he'd created the siren. He laughed and showed me a long reed, which he used for breathing and singing underwater."
"It sounds like he was proud of his trick," Raoul said.

"Oh, he was. In some respects Erik is like a child who craves attention, but I scolded him severely. His trick had almost killed me, and I had no doubt that it had already been fatal to others. I reminded him that he'd promised me no more murders. 'Have I really committed murders?' he asked in a cheerful voice, trying to disarm me."
"And had he?" Raoul asked.
"Oh, yes, back when we both lived in Persia."
"Christine is with a murderer!" Raoul leaped up. "We must rescue her at once!"

"In a few minutes." The Persian motioned for Raoul to sit down. "Erik said he'd rather forget the past, but I reminded him that I'd saved his life years ago. I wanted him to promise again that there would be no more murders, but he refused. 'As you well know,' he said, 'I never keep my promises.'"
Raoul was shocked by what he was hearing. "A woman died when the chandelier fell during the opera. Was that another of Erik's fatal tricks?"

"I asked him about that," the Persian said. "He denied any involvement, saying that the chandelier was old and worn and fell on its own. But he laughed so horribly that I wasn't sure what to believe. He warned me not to try to enter his house again. Then he said he'd hate to have to dedicate his funeral mass to me, which I took as a death threat."
"So, that's why we're not entering the house from the lake," Raoul said.

The Persian nodded. "That entrance is obviously well-guarded, especially since Erik realized I knew about it. But I figured there was another entrance because I'd often seen him disappear in the third cellar."
"And that's where we are right now?"

"Exactly. Ever since I discovered Erik living at the opera house, I've feared that he might hurt someone. Whenever some accident happened, everyone blamed the ghost, but I suspected Erik," the Persian said. "Although people often laughed about the opera ghost, I wondered how they'd react if they knew the phantom was a real person."
"How did you learn about the revolving mirror in Christine's dressing room?"

"Erik told me that he was a changed person since he was loved for himself," the Persian said. "I didn't know what he meant, but I suspected that Christine might be involved. So I hid in the storage room next to her dressing room and listened while he gave her singing lessons. His voice could be as loud as thunder or as soft as an angel's, and it was always beautiful. But I couldn't understand how his voice, no matter how marvelous, could make her forget his frightening face. And then it dawned on me—"
"Christine had not yet seen him!" Raoul finished the Persian's sentence.

"Exactly. Later on I found the trapdoor that enabled Erik to go straight to the cellars from the stage. I also went into Christine's dressing room and discovered the hidden button that moved the mirror. Behind the mirror, I found the passage leading to the spring."
"Christine described to me how he took her through that passage and put her on a white horse," Raoul said.

"So you won't be surprised when I tell you I witnessed him bathing her temples with water at the spring. The white horse, which I'm sure he'd stolen from the opera stables, waited patiently nearby. When I revealed myself, it was terrible. Sparks flew from Erik's eyes, but before I could speak, I received a blow to the head that stunned me."
"You mean he knocked you out?"

"Yes, and when I came to, Erik, Christine, and the horse were gone. I felt sure that Erik had taken that poor girl prisoner and was keeping her in his house. Despite Erik's warnings and threats, I was determined to return to the edge of the lake. I hid there overnight, waiting for him to reappear."
By now Raoul was desperate to leave the third cellar and continue the hunt for Christine. But the Persian still hadn't finished his story.
"I waited by the lake because I figured that Erik would eventually have to go outside to get food and clothing for Christine," he went on.

"Aha!" Raoul's eyes brightened with recognition. "Christine told me that he brought her those things the first morning of her captivity. But how could Erik go shopping without scaring everyone to death? I've seen his face; it looks like a skull."

"Erik has a mask with a fake nose that makes him look almost human," the Persian explained. "But back to that morning. I grew tired of waiting and was beginning to think he must have left by another door. Suddenly I heard oars splashing in the water and saw two glowing yellow eyes. When the boat reached the shore, Erik jumped out."
"Had he spotted you?"

"He walked straight over to me and said, 'You've been waiting here since last night, and you're annoying me. I'm telling you that this will all end badly, and it'll be your fault. You think you're following me, but I'm following you. I've been extraordinarily patient with you, but you don't seem to take the hint!' Erik was so furious that I didn't dare to interrupt him."
"What was he so angry about?" Raoul asked.

"Erik said that if his secrets got out, there would be trouble for everyone. I wasn't sure what he meant, but I tried to reassure him that I was after Christine, not him. Erik replied that he had every right to see Christine in his own house because she loved him."
"That's not true!" Raoul pounded his fist on the cellar floor. "Christine is not in his house because she wants to be. She's there because he carried her off and locked her up again!"

"That's exactly what I said," the Persian said. "Erik thought for a minute and finally said, 'If I prove that she loves me, will you promise not to meddle in my life anymore?' I promised, but I didn't know how on earth he'd be able to prove that."
"So did he find a way?" Raoul wasn't sure he wanted to hear the answer.
"Erik thought if he let Christine leave and then she came back, that would prove she loved him despite his looks. He was positive that she would return to him and then they'd get married."
"What!" Raoul exclaimed. "Christine would never marry Erik! She's engaged to me!"

"You and I know that she loves you," the Persian said. "But Erik was so confident about her love, he'd already composed a wedding mass. He even sang part of it for me. I said I would believe him if I saw Christine leave the house on the lake and return to it voluntarily. I promised, if Erik proved to be right, I'd stop meddling in his affairs."
"I know Christine went back to the house on the lake." Raoul wrinkled his brow as he tried to remember. "But I'm not sure when she—"
"The night of the masked ball."
"Of course! That was when I witnessed her disappearing through the mirror in her dressing room."

"And to my amazement, there were several other times too." The Persian shook his head in disbelief. "I know I'd promised not to interfere, but I felt a responsibility toward Christine. I resolved to be extremely careful and neither return to the lake nor use the passage behind the mirror."
"I appreciate your concern for Christine." Raoul reached out and laid his hand on the Persian's shoulder. "You must have spent a lot of time here, trying to find the entrance to Erik's house."

"I wondered if the death of Joseph Buquet might offer a clue. Perhaps Buquet had seen something that Erik didn't want anyone to know. So I came here—the spot where Buquet's body was found—and waited for hours. One day my patience was rewarded. Erik appeared, knelt down, and pressed a stone in the floor. The stone moved, he dropped through an opening, and the stone slid back into place."
"Did you follow him?"

"I waited for at least thirty minutes before I pressed on the stone. Everything happened just as it did for Erik. But I didn't go through the opening for fear that Erik was waiting in the dark below. I continued to worry about Erik's relationship with Christine as I cautiously wandered through the opera house. That was how I discovered that her heart belonged to you, Monsieur de Chagny. As the two of you rambled through the opera house, little did you suspect that I was watching over you."
"So there was someone following us—and it was you!" Raoul said.

"I was prepared to do anything to keep you safe, but Erik didn't try to threaten you. Still I was not at ease. One day I came back here and moved the stone in the floor. I immediately heard the most astounding music; Erik was at work on his Don Juan Triumphant. All at once I heard him say, 'This must be finished first ! Quite finished!' I didn't know what he was planning, but I remembered him mentioning 'trouble for everyone.' My heart stopped when I read the news of your engagement in today's newspaper. Surely that would prompt Erik to act, and it did—he kidnapped Christine right off the stage. And so, my young friend, we find ourselves about to enter Erik's house. Are you ready?"
"Of course!" Raoul shot to his feet. "But one more question: How was Erik able to build his house undetected?"

"That's easy. He knew every nook and cranny of the opera house because he was one of the chief contractors who built it. And now we must be quiet because once we enter his house, our every word can be overheard."

The Persian ran his hand over the floor and pressed a stone, which slid to the side. Raoul followed the Persian through the opening, lowering himself into the dark room below. The Persian turned on his lantern and checked the ceiling.
"The stone has closed over the opening," the Persian said. "Let's hope there's another way out." He swept his lantern over the walls and floor.
"I don't see any doors," Raoul said. "The walls are covered with mirrors!"
The Persian wiped the sweat from his brow. "Unfortunately, we appear to have dropped into Erik's notorious hexagon room."
Raoul and the Persian had landed in the middle of a small six-sided room with no doors. In one corner stood a tree, which the mirrored walls transformed into an endless forest.
Raoul started to shout his fiancée's name, but the Persian grabbed his arm and motioned for him to be silent.
"I know you want to reassure Christine that help is nearby, but we must speak quietly," the Persian said.
Suddenly the two men heard a noise coming from the next room. It sounded like a door opening and shutting, followed by a moan.
"Christine, you must make your choice," Erik said. "What will it be: the wedding mass or the funeral mass?"
Christine did not respond.
"The funeral mass is dark and solemn," Erik went on, "while the wedding mass is—you can take my word for it—magnificent!"
When Christine stayed silent, the Persian glanced at Raoul, worried that he'd call to her. "Erik obviously doesn't know we're here, or he would have come after us," he whispered.

"I can't go on living like a mole in a burrow!" Erik went on. "I've finished my masterpiece, Don Juan Triumphant , and now I want to live like everybody else. I want to have a wife like any other man and take a Sunday stroll together. I know you dread being seen with me, Christine, but I've created a new mask with a mustache that makes me look like other men. People won't turn to stare at me on the streets anymore. You'll be the happiest of women, and we'll sing together all day long."
Raoul and the Persian heard the sound of Christine crying.
"You're afraid of me, and yet I'm not really wicked," Erik said. "Love me and you'll see."

While Christine continued to cry, Erik wailed, "You don't love me . . . you don't love me . . . you don't love me!" Then in a gentle voice, he said, "You know it pains me to see you cry—why are you crying?"
There was a long silence, which gave Raoul hope. "Maybe Erik has gone into another room," he whispered to the Persian.
"If that's so, then Christine might be able to open the door—wherever that is—and we could rescue her," the Persian said.
But before Raoul could call out to Christine, a doorbell rang on her side of the wall.
"Who's bothering me now?" Erik snapped. "The siren must take care of this visitor."
Upon hearing Erik leave the room, Raoul called out. "Christine! It's Raoul!"
There was a moment's silence before Christine responded. "I must be dreaming. Is that really you, my darling?"
"Yes, the Persian and I have arrived to rescue you, but we're stuck in the hexagon room with no way to reach you. I think you're on the other side of this wall."

"Oh, Raoul!" Christine cried. "Erik has given me until 11 o'clock tomorrow night to make a decision. I must either agree to marry him, or he will do something terrible, which will harm many people! He won't explain what that is, and I'm so afraid!"
"Listen to me," the Persian said. "You must warn us if you hear Erik returning. Do you know where he's gone?"
"I suspect he left the house," Christine said.
"Can you make sure?" the Persian asked.
"No, I can't move," Christine said. "Erik has tied me to a chair in my room."
"This is outrageous!" Raoul muttered.
The Persian realized there was no time to waste. "Leave this to me, sir," he said to Raoul. Then he asked Christine if she could see any doors.
"There are only two doors in my room," Christine said. "Erik comes and goes through one, and he has forbidden me to open the second door. He says that door leads to a room filled with danger."
"I think we're behind the second door," the Persian said, "but we can't see it from this side of the wall."
"If only I could reach the door," Christine said, "I could knock and you'd know exactly where it is."
The two men heard noises that sounded like Christine struggling to free herself.
"Can you see a lock on the door?" the Persian asked.

"Yes, and I know where the key is," Christine said. "It's in a leather bag near the organ in the next room. Erik has forbidden me to touch the bag, which holds another key, a little brass one that he calls the key of life or death. Oh, run, Raoul! Flee while you have the chance because everything is so mysterious and dangerous here."
"No, my dear, I cannot leave you," Raoul said.
"Erik knows that it's impossible for you to escape," the Persian said, "so why has he tied you up?"
"Because I've already attempted to escape, so he's afraid I'll try again," Christine said. "And he knows if I succeed, I won't come back this time."
"Oh, my poor Christine!" Raoul cried.

The Persian took a deep breath while gathering his thoughts. "Mademoiselle, if you ask in the right way, Erik will untie you. You can take advantage of his love for you—smile at him when you tell him that the rope hurts your wrists."
"Hush!" Christine said. "He's coming back! Flee while you can!"
"Be brave! We won't leave until we've rescued you," the Persian said.
Raoul and the Persian heard a door open, and then Christine cried out in horror.

"I apologize for allowing you see my face like this," Erik said, sounding distracted and upset. "It's that man's fault. Why did he have to come to my door? I don't ask for visitors. As for what happened next . . . well, that's the siren's fault."
"Erik has killed someone," the Persian whispered to Raoul.
"Erik, I'm in pain," Christine said. "My wrists—"

"Oh, my poor dear. Of course, I'll release you. Why are you staring at me? Is it because I'm all wet? There you are . . . you're free now. I must go into the next room and play the funeral mass for that man who came to the door."

Soon Raoul and the Persian heard Erik playing the organ while he sang the mass. For a while the sound seemed to envelop them like a storm, but then they heard the sound of running, followed by a whisper. "I've got it!"
Relief flooded through the Persian and Raoul—until abruptly, the music stopped.
"Christine," Erik roared, "what have you done with my leather bag?"
Raoul and the Persian listened in horror as Erik roared at Christine.
"You asked me to untie you so that you could take my bag! You know there's nothing in it except two keys."
"I want to look at this hexagon room that you've kept hidden from me," Christine replied.
"Give me the bag!" As Erik snatched it from Christine, she yelped in pain.
Raoul exploded with rage when he heard her cry out. "No!" he shouted.
"What was that?" Erik demanded.
"I didn't hear anything," Christine said.
"Well, I thought I heard a cry."
"Erik, you and I are the only people here," Christine said, "and I cried out because you hurt my wrist when you took away the bag."

"I don't like the way you said that. Furthermore, you're trembling, and I suspect that's because you're lying to me. I'm certain I heard a cry—there must be someone next door. Perhaps it's the man you want to marry."
"Oh, Erik," Christine said, forcing a laugh. "You know I don't want to marry anybody."
"It won't take long to discover who's in there, and we won't even require the key."
Erik pressed a button, flooding the hexagon room with light from the ceiling. The unexpected switch from total darkness to bright light caused Raoul to stumble.
"Now did you hear a noise?" Erik asked Christine. "There's definitely someone in there, and you're going to find out who it is."

Raoul and the Persian listened as Erik instructed Christine to climb a stepladder. "You've often asked me why there's a ladder in your room, and now you know. It's to give you a peep into the hexagon room. Go ahead and climb up to the little window by the ceiling. I'll turn off the light in here, so no one in the hexagon room will see you."
"I'm afraid of the dark," Christine protested. "Do we need to go to all this effort just because of a little noise?"
But Erik would not permit himself to be distracted. "Fine, if you won't look, then I'll have to investigate myself."
"No, no, I'll look," Christine said.
"Thank you, my darling," Erik said. "It's kind of you to save me the trouble of climbing."
Raoul looked at the Persian and mouthed silently, "What do we do now?"
The Persian shrugged to indicate that he had no idea either.
The two men soon heard Christine's voice above their heads. "No one's there, dear," she called down to Erik.
"Are you quite sure?"
"Yes, I can't see anybody."
"All right, you can come back down," Erik said.
Raoul and the Persian let out quiet sighs of relief.
"What did you think of my forest in the hexagon room?" Erik asked Christine. "Isn't this an amusing house with a landscape like that?"
"It's lovely—such a delightful forest. Did you design that room?" Christine said, hoping that flattery would placate Erik. "You're such a gifted artist."

"Yes, I designed the whole house, but I'm sick and tired of having a forest in my house. I want a nice, quiet apartment with ordinary doors and windows as well as a wife to love. I'd take her out on Sundays and keep her amused on weekdays—I can be very amusing, you know."

Raoul listened in horror as Erik went on talking to Christine. "Shall I show you some card tricks to help pass the time while we wait for 11 o'clock tomorrow night? My dear Christine, tell me you love me! No, wait, I know you don't love me now, but you will. Plenty of young people who didn't care for each other before marriage have learned to love each other. Have I told you that I'm a ventriloquist—the finest ventriloquist who ever lived?"
The Persian leaned toward Raoul and whispered in his ear, "It sounds as if Erik is trying to distract her from something."

Christine had sensed that something bad was connected to the light. "Erik, is there really any need for that bright light in the hexagon room? I've already looked and seen nothing there, so maybe you could turn it out."

"Not now, my dear. Let me demonstrate my skills as a ventriloquist. I'll raise my mask just a little, so you can see that my mouth—such as it is—never moves. And yet you can hear my voice. Where should my voice come from . . . the leather bag? How about the little box on the right on your mantelpiece? Or the little box on the left? One of those ebony boxes is quite safe, but the other—"
"I'm still wondering about that light," Christine interrupted him. "Don't you think you could put it out?"

"Not now, dear," Erik said. "Don't you want to hear how I made Carlotta croak when she sang? One minute my voice was coming from her throat, and the next it was on a chair in box five, telling the managers, 'Carlotta is singing to bring down the chandelier!' And where is my voice now, darling Christine? It's in the hexagon room saying, 'Woe to him who has a real nose and has come to snoop around Erik's house!'"
Raoul looked at the Persian in terror. "Erik knows we're in here!" he said. "He was only pretending to be satisfied when Christine said no one was here."

Suddenly Erik's terrible voice was everywhere. It passed through the wall and surrounded his captives, who felt that he was in the room with them. Raoul and the Persian put their hands over their ears, but they couldn't block out that horrible sound.
Just when they thought they couldn't bear it for another second, Christine said, "Erik, I'm tired of listening to your voice, and it's sweltering in here."
"Yes, the heat is unbearable," Erik said.
"This wall feels like it's on fire," Christine said, patting the wall. "What's going on?"
"It's from the forest next door."
"What does that have to do with anything?"
Erik laughed loudly and hideously. "Didn't you notice that it was a tropical forest?"
"It's not the forest," Christine said. "The heat is coming from the light and the walls."

With the heat increasing, Raoul shouted and banged on the walls. The Persian made no attempt to restrain him as they heard Erik dragging Christine away. A door slammed, and then, as the temperature continued to rise, there was silence.

"We must get out of here!" Raoul said to the Persian as the temperature kept rising in the hexagon room. While the Persian sat calmly on the floor, Raoul paced the mirrored room with the forest on its walls. "Can't we go back the way we came in?"

"As soon as we entered, the stone closed over the opening," the Persian reminded him. "And now the light coming from the ceiling is so bright that I can't even look up. Besides, there's no way for us to reach the ceiling."
Sweat ran down Raoul's face as he proposed another solution. "Why don't we try escaping through the forest?"

The Persian realized that the heat was beginning to affect Raoul's mind. "You must remember that the forest is an optical illusion created by Erik. Keep reminding yourself that we are in a little room and that we'll soon escape. If you stop pacing and let me concentrate, I can probably open the door to Christine's room in less than an hour."
Raoul sat down, pretending he was on the forest floor. "The view is splendid from here," he said.

The Persian ignored his delirious companion's remarks and set to work, systematically examining the six mirrors. Knowing Erik, the Persian decided that there must be a tiny button that made one mirror turn like a revolving door. But where was it? After half an hour, the Persian had carefully inspected three panels and still hadn't found anything.
Raoul moaned. "If we stay here much longer, we'll be roasted alive. How long before you open that door?"

The Persian turned away from the mirror he'd been examining. "I'm halfway around the room, so it won't be much longer. Now where was I?" To his horror, the Persian suddenly realized he'd lost his place and would have to start over.

Meanwhile Raoul was beginning to see things. "There's Christine between those trees over there. Christine, I've been looking for you for so long! Come here, my darling. Now I've lost you again. Oh, I'm thirsty!"
As for the Persian, he was so thirsty that he felt as if his throat were on fire. Yet he kept hunting for the invisible door.
"Christine! Where are you?" Raoul called again. "Night is coming!"
Although a moon appeared in the fading light, it grew even hotter in the room. From somewhere nearby came the roar of a lion.

"Don't be afraid! It's only another of Erik's tricks," the Persian said to Raoul. "He's a master of sound effects, and usually follows the lion with the snarling of a leopard and the buzzing of a fly."
The two men did not hear any more creatures in the night, but they did see something different. The scene before them changed from moonlit forest to sunbaked desert.
"A desert!" Raoul cried. "It's only going to get hotter."
"Remember, it's not real," the Persian said to Raoul. "Erik controls everything we see and hear."
"If it's not real, then how does he do it?" Raoul asked.
"I'm not entirely sure."

At that moment it occurred to the Persian that Erik was probably nearby. "By now, I'm sure Erik knows who's in his hexagon room," the Persian said to himself. "Maybe I should try to negotiate with him." The Persian shouted Erik's name, but no one responded.
"What will become of us in this endless desert?" Raoul asked. "Aren't you thirsty?"
Indeed the Persian was beginning to think they would die of thirst when Raoul suddenly pointed to a spot on the horizon. "Look! An oasis!"

Far in the distance the Persian saw a pool of water. For a moment his hopes rose, but then he recognized it as the worst of Erik's cruel tricks. "There's no water," he said. "It's a mirage, just another trick of the mirrors."

"I don't want to hear anything more about tricks or mirrors or revolving doors!" Raoul dragged himself along the floor. "The desert is real and so is the water. Why, I can even hear the water flowing."

The Persian had to admit that he, too, heard the sound of river water gurgling over rocks. There was another welcome sound too. "Do you hear rain, Raoul?" he asked. "I know that Erik is perfectly capable of imitating the sound of falling rain, but that sounds real."

Desperate for something to drink, the men dragged themselves to the imaginary riverbank. When they reached the mirror, they stuck out their tongues to lap up some refreshing water. The glass was burning hot!
"Ow! My tongue!" Raoul screamed.

The Persian closed his eyes and rolled on the floor in pain. When he opened his eyes, he spotted something in a groove in the floor. The button! He'd been searching the mirrors when all this time, the button was in the floor.
"Watch this!" the Persian said to Raoul as he pressed the button.

But to their surprise, a door did not open in the wall. Instead cool air flowed up to them as a trapdoor in the floor slid open. The two men leaned over the opening, drinking in the cool air as if it were water.
"What do you think is down there?" Raoul asked.
The Persian reached into the darkness and felt one step and then another. "A winding stone staircase."
Raoul wanted to hurry down the stairs, but the Persian stopped him.
"Not so fast," the older man said. "It may be another trick of Erik's. Let me go first with my lantern."
With the Persian in the lead, the two men slowly descended into the darkness. At the bottom of the stairs, the Persian swung his lantern around a room full of barrels.
"I hope they're all full of water," Raoul said.
"Let me use my knife to pry this one open," the Persian said. As the two men worked on the barrel, they heard a voice calling out to them.
"Barrels . . . barrels . . . any barrels to sell?"
"That's weird," Raoul said. "It sounded as if the barrel were singing."
The two men looked all around the barrel. "There's nothing here." The Persian frowned. "Our senses must be playing tricks on us after all that time in the heat."
They went back to working on the barrel and at last pried it open. Raoul dipped his hands into the barrel and cried out, "This isn't water! It's gunpowder!"

Fearing that his lantern might cause the barrel of gunpowder to explode, the Persian tossed it aside. It broke, leaving the Persian and Raoul in the dark. They couldn't even rely on the light shining through the open trapdoor because it had been switched off.

"We must return to the hexagon room and try to speak with Christine." The Persian stumbled against a barrel. "With our discovery of the gunpowder, I finally understand Erik's threat. If Christine doesn't agree to marry him, he'll blow up the opera house at eleven o'clock tomorrow night!"
Raoul was stunned. "At that hour the opera house will be full of people! But Christine will never agree to spend the rest of her life with such a monster."
"I don't think she realizes the life-or-death consequences of her decision," the Persian said as they carefully climbed the stairs to the hexagon room.
"Eleven o'clock tomorrow night." Raoul repeated as the two men sat on the floor in total darkness.
"I wonder what time it is," the Persian said. "My watch has stopped."
"It seems like we've been stuck in this mirrored prison for years," Raoul put his watch up to his ear. "Mine is still ticking, but I can't see the hands to tell the time."
"Break the glass and touch the hands."
Raoul did as he was told. "Judging by the space between the hands, I'd say it's almost 11 o'clock."
"But is that morning or the evening?"

"I don't know! Who could keep track of time when we were in the forest? Or in the desert?" Raoul's voice grew louder as he became more frustrated. "We may have 12 hours until Erik's explosion or only a few minutes. I have no idea."
"Hush!" the Persian said. "I hear footsteps coming from Christine's room next door."
"Raoul, Raoul!" Christine said. "Is that you I hear? Are you still alive?"
"Yes, my darling."

"Oh, thank goodness." Christine began to sob with relief. "I promised to marry Erik if he took me to the hexagon room, but he refused. He said there was no more need for that key and threw it in the lake. He's gone out for a few minutes to give me time to decide whether to marry him or not. Oh, Raoul, I thought you were dead. I thought—"
"Mademoiselle! What time is it?" the Persian interrupted.
"Five minutes before 11."
"Yes, but in the morning or the evening?"

"The evening. It's five minutes before I must make my decision. Oh, Raoul, I'm so frightened. Erik tore off his mask, and his eyes shot yellow flames. Then he handed me the other key from his leather bag—the brass one—and said it opens both ebony boxes on my mantel. He called it the key of life or death. I don't understand why he said that, but—"
"It must have something to do with the gunpowder," the Persian said.

"Gunpowder?" Christine paused. "Erik didn't say anything about gunpowder. He said one box contained a brass scorpion and the other a brass grasshopper. If I turned the scorpion around, that meant I'd marry him. But if I turned the grasshopper, that meant my answer was no. His last words were 'Be careful of the grasshopper. It hops! It hops really high!'"
"You know Erik," Raoul said to the Persian. "What do you think he means about the grasshopper hopping really high?"
"I have no doubt that the grasshopper controls an electric current that will blow up the barrels of gunpowder."
"Why do you keep talking about gunpowder?" Christine asked.
Raoul quickly explained the situation to his fiancée and urged her to turn the scorpion at once.
"No! Don't touch the scorpion!" the Persian cried.
"What?" Raoul said.

"This may be another trick of Erik's," the Persian said. "He couldn't really expect Christine to marry him, so perhaps he gave her the wrong information. Maybe he's hiding somewhere, waiting to watch the opera house explode from a safe distance."
"Here he comes!" Christine said.
The two men heard Erik's footsteps as he entered the room next door.
"Hello, Erik!" the Persian called out boldly.

With extraordinary calmness, Erik replied, "So you're not dead in there." The Persian tried to reply, but Erik silenced him. "Not a word or I shall blow up everything, and that honor belongs to Mademoiselle Christine. I see that she has not touched the scorpion or the grasshopper, but it's not too late to do the right thing. Give me the key, my dear."

Erik laughed wickedly and opened the two boxes for Christine. "Let's look at both creatures, shall we? Aren't they pretty? If you choose the grasshopper, we shall all be blown up because there is enough gunpowder under our feet to destroy the whole neighborhood. But if you choose the scorpion, the gunpowder will be soaked with water and made useless. All those Parisians upstairs listening to a second-rate opera will be forever grateful to you for saving their lives. And we shall be happily married!"
Erik paused. "If you haven't turned the scorpion in two minutes, I will turn the grasshopper."
There was a long, terrible silence during which Raoul prayed and the Persian listened to his heart pounding.
"Your two minutes are up," Erik announced. "Good-bye, Christine. Hop, grasshopper!"
"Wait!" Christine cried. "Do you promise that the scorpion is the right one to turn?"
"Yes, but if you won't turn it now, I'll turn the grasshopper."
"Erik!"
"Enough!" Erik roared.
"Erik! I've turned the scorpion!"

The Persian and Raoul heard a hissing noise beneath their feet as water flowed into the room below them. They had forgotten their thirst, but now they ran to the bottom of the steps and drank and drank. As the water rose, they retreated up the staircase, step by step. The water came out of the cellar and flooded the floor of the hexagon room.
"Erik, that's enough water. The gunpowder is soaked," the Persian called out. "Turn off the tap."
"Christine, the water is up to our knees!" Raoul said.
But Erik did not reply and neither did Christine.

The Persian and Raoul were alone in the dark with the water rising and no one to turn off the tap. They lost their footing and were thrown against the mirrors as the water spun them around the hexagon room.
"I love you, Christine!" Raoul called.
"Erik, remember that I saved your life!" the Persian cried, but it was too late. The water filled the room, and the two men lost consciousness.

When the Persian regained consciousness, he was lying in bed, and Raoul was nearby, asleep on a sofa. An angel and a devil—Christine and Erik—were watching over them. The Persian raised himself on one elbow and looked around the room. "Where are we?"

"You're in Christine's room in my house," Erik replied. "As is the viscount. He woke up long before we knew if you were still alive, but we must let him sleep now. Soon I will take you up to the surface of the earth to please my wife."

The Persian was startled by those last words, but they had no effect on Christine, who sat quietly reading. Erik gave the Persian something to drink and warned him not to speak to Christine or Raoul. The next thing the Persian knew, he was waking up in his own bed at home.
"How did I get here?" the Persian asked his servant, Darius, who was standing by the bed.
"Someone rang the doorbell last night, sir," Darius said. "When I answered the door, you were the only person there, and you were unconscious."

Hoping that Raoul had also been brought home, the Persian sent a message to his house. But the reply that came back was upsetting: Raoul was missing, and his brother, Philippe, was dead. The count's body had been found on the edge of the lake underneath the opera house.

"How terrible!" the Persian muttered, rereading the note. From what he knew about Erik and things Raoul had told him, he pieced together what had happened. When Philippe thought Christine and Raoul had eloped, he went after them. Failing to find them, Philippe had dashed back into the opera house and entered the cellars, where he became the siren's victim. The Persian shuddered, remembering Erik's playing of the funeral mass.
He rang for his servant. "Darius, help me get dressed, and then summon a cab. I must go to the police at once."

But the police did not take the Persian's evidence seriously. A murderer and kidnapper was living by the lake under the opera house? How was that possible? And so the Persian returned home, determined to write down his story and hand it to the newspapers. While he was writing, a mysterious man appeared at his apartment, demanding to see him.
"The stranger won't tell me his name or show his face," Darius reported to the Persian. "He refuses to leave until he has spoken to you."
"Send him in," the Persian said to his servant. "I know who it is."
The Persian rose to his feet as Erik entered his drawing room. Erik looked extremely weak and leaned against the wall as if he was afraid of falling.
"Murderer of Count Philippe, what have you done with Raoul and Christine?" the Persian demanded.
Erik staggered under this direct attack and dragged himself to a chair. "Don't talk to me about Philippe. The siren caused him to have an unfortunate accident, and he fell into the lake."
"Liar!" the Persian shouted.
Erik bowed his head. "I haven't come here to talk about Philippe, but to tell you that I'm dying. I'm—"
"Where are Christine and Raoul?"

Erik ignored the Persian's question and went on, gasping for breath. "I'm dying of love. I've always loved Christine, and I love her now more than ever. You should have heard how she begged me to release you and Raoul. She promised to marry me if I spared your lives, so I carried you here."
"Answer me!" the Persian shouted. "Are Christine and Raoul alive?"

"Of course they are. After I took you home, I chained Raoul in a dungeon under the opera house. And then . . ." Erik was momentarily overcome with emotion. "And then Christine let me kiss her on the forehead! You can't imagine what that was like for me. My poor, unhappy mother would never let me kiss her. She used to toss me my mask and run away. Nor has any other woman ever allowed me to kiss her. I was so happy that I cried and fell at Christine's feet. And when I looked up, Christine was crying too!"
As the Persian watched Erik sob, tears of pity came to his own eyes. "He's committed some terrible crimes," the Persian thought, "but what a sad, unfortunate man."

Erik took a deep breath and began again. "When I felt Christine's tears on my forehead, I removed my mask so I wouldn't lose a single one of her tears. And she didn't run away! She stayed with me, weeping over me, weeping with me. At that moment I felt all the happiness the world had to offer."

Erik began coughing and sputtering. "I heard Christine say, 'Poor, unhappy Erik!' and she took my hand. I had found the gold ring that she'd lost after I'd given it to her. I slipped the ring on her hand and told her to take it for herself and for Raoul. When she asked what I meant, I told her I was releasing her from her promise to marry me. She could marry Raoul whenever she wanted because she had cried with me."
At that point Erik told the Persian not to look at him. "I have to remove my mask because I'm choking."

The Persian walked over to the window and opened it. His heart was full of pity, but he kept his eyes on the scene outside his window. When he heard Erik take a deep breath and put the mask back on, he turned around and found Erik ready to continue talking.

"I immediately brought Raoul to Christine, and they kissed in front of me. I made Christine promise to wear my ring until she learned of my death, when she should go to my house and bury the ring with my body. Then Christine kissed me right here!" Erik tapped his forehead. "She and Raoul hurried off together, making plans for their wedding, and leaving me—the only person still crying—alone."
The Persian was no longer worried about Christine and Raoul because he had no doubt that Erik was telling the truth. He had no further questions for Erik, who rose to leave.
"I do have one final request," Erik said at the door. "When I feel the end is near, I will notify you. Then you must put an ad in the newspaper so the young couple will know that I have died."
Three weeks later an ad appeared in one of the Paris newspapers: "Erik is dead."

With Erik's death, the strange story of the opera ghost ended. Yet for quite some time, people kept talking about events such as Christine's kidnapping, Philippe's death, and Raoul's disappearance. Christine never sang again in public. Many in Paris assumed that she was the victim of a rivalry between Raoul and Philippe. None knew the truth—she and Raoul had escaped to a life of quiet happiness. And few wondered about Mama Valerius, who had vanished at the same time as the young couple. A newspaper blamed the opera ghost for everything that had happened.

Of course, other mysterious events occurred at the opera house that were never mentioned in the press. One day Richard and Moncharmin, the managers, found a large envelope in their office. It contained the forty thousand francs the opera ghost had taken from Richard's pocket, plus a note written in red ink: "With many thanks, the OG." Although relieved to receive the money, each manager privately blamed the other for its disappearance.

There was only one person in Paris who knew the truth about everything that had happened. And years later the Persian revealed some of those secrets to an opera house historian. They sat together in the Persian's drawing room.

"Erik was easily able to torment the managers," the Persian began. "Because box five contained an enormous column that appeared to be made of solid marble. However, it was actually made of wood painted to look like stone. Erik could hide inside it. And as a master ventriloquist, he could make his voice sound like it was coming from anywhere in the box."

The Persian said that box five also contained a small, movable panel. Erik used it to leave notes and tips for Madame Giry. He had reached through a similar panel in the floor of the managers' office to pick Richard's pocket.
The historian looked up from taking notes. "So Erik was simply amusing himself by demanding payments from the managers?"

"No, Erik felt the world owed him something as compensation for his appearance," the Persian said. "But when he was dying from a broken heart, after he had freed Christine from their engagement, he was no longer interested in anything, including money."
The historian asked how Erik came to be living underneath the opera house.

"Erik was born in northern France to a master mason and his wife," the Persian said. "At an early age, he ran away from home because his appearance horrified his parents. He was even exhibited at fairs as 'the living corpse' before his other talents were known."
"What a terrible life! Can you tell me something about Erik's other talents?"
"Erik sang divinely and was good at ventriloquism and magic tricks. Word of his talents spread across Europe and as far as Persia. That's where I first met him."

The Persian took a sip of tea. "The shah ordered me to find Erik and bring him to Persia. As the chief of police, I was horrified by this unusual man, and I am not speaking of his appearance. Erik seemed to have no sense of right and wrong. He also took part in a number of political assassinations for the shah. But he was more than a murderer."
"What do you mean?"

"Erik had unusual ideas about architecture that incorporated his love of magic. He built a palace full of trapdoors and hidden passages. This enabled the shah to move about unseen and to mysteriously appear and disappear."
The historian smiled. "That must have delighted the shah."

The Persian nodded. "But the shah feared that Erik might build a similar palace for another ruler. He decided that Erik must die, so that no one would discover the secrets of his palace. I was ordered to carry out this terrible assignment, but I couldn't bring myself to do it. Instead I helped Erik escape. When we met again in Paris, Erik seemed to forget that I had saved his life."

The Persian went on. "Meanwhile the shah was furious at me. He took all my property and banished me from Persia. Fortunately, I continued to receive a small pension, so I could live in Paris. As for Erik, he fled to another country. There he built a second palace full of trapdoors and secret chambers."
"How did he get to Paris?" the historian asked.
"Once again he had to disappear because he knew too much. Tired of his adventurous life, he wanted to settle down in Paris. He became a builder here."
The historian put down his pen. "I'm guessing that he must have had a hand in building the opera house."

"That's correct," the Persian said. "In Paris he first worked as an ordinary contractor constructing ordinary buildings. When he saw the plans for the opera house, he bid on the construction of the foundation, and his bid was accepted. Suddenly he began to dream of creating a dwelling for his own use, hidden deep in the cellar walls. He imagined he could live peacefully here, far away from curiosity seekers."
"I've searched for his house on the lake, but I've never been able to find it," the historian said.
"One of Erik's final acts before he died was to block up all the secret entrances." The Persian covered a yawn.
"Just one more question, and then I'll leave you in peace," the historian said. "What did you think of Erik?"

The Persian put his fingertips together. "First, I'd like to emphasize that Erik was a real person and not a ghost. I can't forget that he did many horrifying things in his life. He was a murderer, who terrorized many people including Raoul, Christine, and me."
"And yet you and Christine felt some pity for him. Why?"

The Persian stayed silent for a long time. "All Erik wanted was to be loved like anyone else. Alas, his appearance frightened people and made that impossible. So he turned his genius and creativity toward evil—playing tricks and hurting people." The Persian lowered his voice. "I've often wondered what he could have accomplished if he hadn't been disfigured and unloved since birth. Because beneath Erik's hideous exterior was . . ."
"Yes?" the historian prodded him.
"An artist," the Persian concluded. "A brilliant artist who loved beauty and music as much as he loved Christine."
